questions.question: What does the birthday problem ask for?
options: The probability that at least two people in a group share a birthday
The probability that someone in the group shares one given person's birthday
The probability that all people in the group have different birthdays
The probability that exactly one pair in the group shares a birthday

questions.question: What assumptions are used in the simplified birthday problem?
options: Birthdays are independent, with more births in summer than in winter
Birthdays are sampled without replacement from the calendar
Birthdays are independent and uniformly distributed over $365$ days
Birthdays are uniformly distributed over $366$ days, including 29 February

questions.question: Why is the complement useful in the birthday problem?
options: It lets the match probabilities of all pairs simply be added
It removes the need for equally likely birthdays
It is easier to count the event that everyone shares one birthday
It is easier to compute the probability of no match

questions.question: For $n$ draws from $m$ equally likely labels, what is the no-match probability?
options: $\frac{m(m-1)\cdots(m-n+1)}{m^n}$
$\frac{m^n}{m(m-1)\cdots(m-n+1)}$
$\frac{n}{m}$
$1-\frac{n}{m}$

questions.question: What broader situations use the same birthday-problem calculation?
options: Only biological birthdays
Only card draws without replacement.
Hash collisions, repeated IDs, and sampled labels
Only continuous waiting times, which use a different model

questions.question: For $n=2$ people and $365$ possible birthdays, what is the probability of no shared birthday?
For $n=2$ people, what is the probability that they share a birthday under the simplified model?
What is the complement of 'at least two people share a birthday'?
options: Everyone has the same birthday
All birthdays are different
Exactly two people share a birthday
No birthdays are observed

questions.question: Under the usual simplified assumptions, what is notable about a group of $23$ people?
options: At least two of the $23$ people are guaranteed to share a birthday
The probability that someone shares your own birthday is above one half
The probability of at least one shared birthday is about $23/365$
The probability of at least one shared birthday exceeds one half

questions.question: If $1000$ IDs are sampled with replacement from a million possible IDs, what kind of risk is being modeled?
options: A permutation without replacement only
A continuous density calculation
A birthday-type collision risk
A deterministic guarantee of no repeats

questions.question: Why does intuition often underestimate birthday-type collisions?
options: The number of people grows quickly relative to the number of days
Real birthdays are spread more evenly than the uniform model assumes
The number of pairs grows quickly as the group size increases
Each new person multiplies the no-match probability by the same factor

questions.question: What role does independence play in the usual birthday formula?
options: It lets the match probabilities of different pairs be added
It means birthdays are sampled without replacement
It lets the probabilities of successive choices be multiplied
It ensures each person is equally likely to be born on any day

questions.question: Why is the no-match numerator $m(m-1)\cdots(m-n+1)$?
options: It counts ordered label assignments with no repeated label
It counts unordered sets of $n$ distinct labels, as in $\binom{m}{n}$
It counts all ordered assignments, including those with repeats
It counts assignments in which exactly one label is repeated

questions.question: For $n=3$ draws from $m$ equally likely labels, what is the no-match probability?
For $n$ people, how do you express the probability of at least one shared birthday from the no-match probability $q$?
For $3$ people and $365$ days, which expression is the probability of at least one shared birthday?
Why does the standard formula fail if birthdays are not uniformly distributed?
options: The sample space stops being finite
The complement event no longer exists
The equal-label assumption no longer holds
Pairwise comparisons of birthdays become impossible.

questions.question: What happens to the no-match probability if $n>m$ for $n$ draws from $m$ labels?
options: It becomes $1$ because all labels are used
It becomes negative because some factors $m-k$ are negative
It becomes $0$ because at least one label must repeat
It is undefined because sampling more than $m$ labels is not permitted

questions.question: Suppose $4$ IDs are sampled with replacement from $10$ equally likely labels. Which expression gives the collision probability?
options: $1-\frac{10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7}{10^4}$
$\frac{10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7}{10^4}$
$1-\frac{9\cdot8\cdot7\cdot6}{10^4}$
$1-\frac{10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7}{4!\cdot10^4}$

questions.question: If a short-code system samples labels uniformly with replacement, what change reduces birthday-type collision risk?
options: Reducing $m$ while keeping the same number of samples
Increasing the number $m$ of possible labels
Ignoring repeated labels in the data
Making the labels distinct boxes
